The Myth of Liberated Labor: A Short Critique of AI Optimism The video sells itself as a soothing, data-driven analysis of the AI revolution. It uses historical examples (ATMs, elevators) to prove that technology will not take our jobs, but rather free us from routine tasks and turn us into "super-workers." However, upon closer inspection, the text reveals itself as a masterpiece of neoliberal ideology. It perfectly distracts from the actual questions of power and property, psychologically preparing the working class for the next stage of self-exploitation. Here are the four biggest rhetorical tricks of the text: 1. The ATM Myth: "Augmentation" is Just Another Word for Intensification The video celebrates the example of bank tellers: ATMs took over the routine work, so the employees had time for "more complex tasks." In the reality of capitalism, this "augmentation" simply means work intensification. Those "more complex tasks" consisted of aggressively cross-selling credit cards and high-interest loans. The time saved by the machine was not given to the workers as leisure; it was filled by capital with even more profit maximization. 2. The Productivity Trap: Who Owns the 520% More Output? The video calculates that AI can give a worker a 10% productivity gain, which compounds to 520% more output in a year. This is presented as a personal gain. What is completely ignored: Who owns this surplus value? The worker? No, their wage stays the same. The 520% more value flows directly to the owners of the AI and the server farms. The video celebrates the increase in the rate of exploitation, while pretending that AI is a neutral tool that makes the worker "more powerful." 3. The Illusion of "New Jobs": Quantity Over Quality The video cites data showing that 60% of today's jobs did not exist 50 years ago (e.g., dog psychiatrists, wind turbine technicians). Therefore, technology creates more jobs than it destroys. This is a cynical survivorship bias. It ignores the precarity of new mass jobs. While we marvel at niche jobs, the majority of the working class is being pushed into the gig economy (like the Uber drivers mentioned in the video itself, 96% of whom quit within a year). Technology has automated secure middle-class jobs and forced the rest into insecure, poorly paid service roles. 4. Discipline Through Fear: "Learn AI, or It's Your Fault" The core sentence of the video: "Someone using AI will take your job if you do not use AI." This is the purest disciplinary tool of late capitalism. Systemic risks (monopolization, profit pressure) are completely shifted onto the individual. If you lose your job, it’s not because of the greed of shareholders, but because you weren't flexible enough. The pressure for constant self-optimization is masked as personal freedom. Conclusion: The Philosophy of Constant Self-Optimization The video tells us at its core: "Don't be afraid of the machine. Be afraid of your own obsolescence. You just have to think harder and more complexly to compete with it." It replaces the political question "Who owns technological progress and who benefits from it?" with the individualistic question "How fast can you adapt?". It is not a neutral analysis, but a subtle call for capitulation—with the goal of preventing us from seeing through the game of technological exploitation and finally changing its rules.

0:27 Typescript is more commonly used by now than plain JavaScript. Chat GPT thinks that doing type checking on JavaScript using JSDoc type annotations rather that explicitly using .ts files is a growing trend, used in early builds of Visual Studio Code (where Typescript came from) and parts of Node.js So something like this in add.js: // @ts-check /** * @param {number} a * @param {number} b * @returns {number} */ function add(a, b) { return a + b; } Rather than this in add.ts: function add(a: number, b: number): number { return a + b; } The advantage is you can add typing gradually to an existing project, and you don't need to build before release, you can run it directly, because it's just JavaScript with comments. Though often build systems strip comments before deploying so the type checking has to come first. But even though it is just JavaScript, it can be as as statically type safe if you type check it, because actually the type checking done by '// @ts-check' is done by Typescript. Obviously this only works if you annotate your types, but the same is true of regular Typescript, as explicitly declaring types is also optional in Typescript. Sort of. What actually happens is undeclared types are inferred in Typescript. This also happens when JavaScript is type checked via JSDoc and // @ts-check But the results in some cases are less precise because there is less information available to infer types. But if you annotate everything, it's just as strict.
